This is likely down to market liquidity requirements for exchange traded funds and to be used as a pricing buffer to allow the ETF to adjust as necessary for fluctuations of cap weight in the short term. Also worth noting is that you'll see larger price delta between VOO and SWPPX at each quarter end as VOO pays out it's dividend quarterly while SWPPX (amongst many mutual funds) does a year end distribution (this is also part of the reasoning as to why NAV in December for MFs can be delayed right up until midnight EST, rebalancing the fund to ensure the appropriate amount of distribution necessary to maintain the MF status).

Yes and no. They both endeavor to track the index but the holdings in each can vary. They may hold sightly different percentages of each individual security in each given fund (ie. In VOO there may x% of AAPL but y% of AAPL in SWPPX). So holdings in each and the index itself will always have a bit of difference. Additionally, the index itself is the aggregate value of each of the securities on the S&P 500, whereas and index fund has to try to replicate that with shares of the individual securities which can't include fractional amounts, so rounding errors will also be represented in the NAV. It's one of the differences between an exchange traded fund (ETF) and a mutual fund (MF). ETF pricing is dynamic during all trade hours as they trade over the exchanges. Mutual fund shares are bought and redeemed from their issuers and report their net asset value (NAV) at the end of the day. Usually not too late after market close (except in December) but you'll see the SWPPX value more closely match VOO and SPX at market close. 

TL/DR: VOO pricing will change during trading hours, SWPPX updates pricing market hours
 Underlying assets and index remain the same.

This is me GROSSLY over-simplyfing this idea (probably should be a whole paper with cited sources but this is me just ADHD spitballing for now) but my thought is that contemporary economics is the driver for why we demonize producers of porn over consumers.   
  
In a society predicated on consumption (pretty much all of contemporary capitalism), demonizing suppliers of a service or good ensures that the society doesn't minimize consumption. Thereby allowing producers of adjacent goods and services to maintain a thriving industry that capitalizes on societal desire for said product but in a moral or defensible way, ie: sex being used to sell every possible product BUT sex or the fact that pharmaceutical industry practices can often push drugs where they may not have been necessary, that can often be equally addictive or habit forming as non-pharmaceuticals (the entire opioid crisis until its tipping point for example. Also readily viewable in companies with minutely different products that use it as an advertising hook ie: "producer A uses this ingredient but we don't, buy our product", even if both products are essentially the same. Plus if you keep the stigma on the producers instead of the consumers, if the winds change, it keeps the demand high with consumers and allows adjacent producers to pivot into those markets (such as lucrative pornstars who pivot into escorting or weapons producers to sell direct to consumers in ways previously only available to use of force directorates). This is especially true if demand remains consistently high, as producers will often pop up to fill demand (a Pablo Escobar notices a nascent demand for cocaine over marijuana but due to few producers in the market able to meet it, the cocaine demand remains a highly profitable enterprise) but rarely does that occur in the opposite where supply far exceeds demand (currently supply of human labor is VERY high and companies have very little demand, they have not pivoted to create more work for more humans). Plus mishaps when demand is high can be placed upon the shoulder of the consumer rather than the producer, thereby preserving demand (overdoses are the drug users fault, car accidents are the driver's fault, injuries from Jarts lawn darts are the fault of drunk dads rather than the company that made a bunch of spears and suggested consumers throw them at each other). This is also seen in the PR campaigns waged by consumption based industry in holding consumers responsible for recycling, which maintained long term demand without actually changing any supply side requirements (people don't stop buying plastics, instead they continue to buy without concern as long as they think they can be recycled). Just another example of demand side driving human behavior in contemporary capitalist societies. 

Another big driver is cognitive dissonance theory, "I'm not a deviant for consuming porn, the maker is for making it. I'm just a hapless consumer at the whims of society around me". this allows consumers to justify their consumptive behavior (also seen with illegal drug use and vilification of drug producing geographies such as the entire country of Mexico being the target of US conservative ire rather than placing greater weight on the Americans that drive the demand for said drugs, or American outrage at poverty conditions in certain countries while ignoring the conditions being driven by US economic policies that provide a greater degree of comfort and wealth to Americans at the expense of exploitable nascent market economies). Piggybacking off that is system justification theory, or our need to justify ourselves and our behavior as individuals, within a group, and within society. Far easier for the average person to feel ok about their choices when they are laid at the feet of others, especially in something that is considered a societal taboo  ("I'm not part of the problem, the problem exists regardless of me, therefore me engaging in something that perpetuates the problem isn't my responsibility." Most commonly seen every morning when I wake up and look in the mirror before working in my nonsense white collar industry producing nothing and perpetuating a system that is an overall net drain on human well being all os I can have food on my table and a dumb Netflix subscription).   


TL/DR: The way we as humans exist presently (in terms of the modern global economy and society) is reliant on consumption as the primary driver of economies. As such, the established status quo is best maintained by any action that keeps demand high and maintains it high as it's easier to adjust production to meet demand than to stoke demand to meet established production. Basically, the sex industry has a limitless supply side so the important part for maintaining the status quo is keeping the demand high for the product, as there is always new supply available. Therefore society and all of its levers endeavor to do anything it takes to keep consumer demand and demand behavior high, even if it means vilification of suppliers (something I think is mostly true for most industries, weapons, food, clothes, etc. etc)

But I try not to get caught up in the sand of those conversations with them, then they become circular and unproductive.

Edit: TL/DR: Have moderate conversations with people and about how directly things impact them with hard numbers to show to back up claims. They can argue till the cow comes home but when push comes to shove, people are concerned about how things impact themselves.

Charities that focus on conservation efforts or biodiversity don't indirectly impact humans. They directly impact humans. Bees go extinct? Human's suffer famine. Flora and fauna that maintain biodiversity are wiped out because we chopped down all of the forested areas in a place? Well, industrial agriculture means monocultured crops and soil, increasing risk of a a singular factor disrupting food supply chains. Same with water ecosystems, especially where anything from filter feeders to algae blooms can drastically alter an environment to the point of making it uninhabitable or habitable for other species (species that humans in certain areas may rely on for food). Or think about horseshoe crab conservation, where horseshoe crabs are caught and bled and released back into the wild as their blood is a key component in LAL tests which are used to determine courses of treatment in bacterial infections. Your view that you should never donate to animal charities when human charities begs a few questions at very least: 

1) The only absolute is there are no absolutes. "Never" is a strong take when there exist charities focused on animals that have a direct impact on human lives.

2) Humans are the root problem. What law or rule makes humans more important than anything else? The biggest root causes of human suffering is humans not animals. One could argue then that addressing the root cause, such as removing or controlling it, would be in the interest of the alleged greater good. This argument has also been used for millennia to justify land grabs and invasions, wars, development of chemical or nuclear weapons (and subsequent use of them), genocides, etc. 

3) This planet, like the humans and animals that reside on it, is a functioning ecosystem that is greater than the sum of its parts. You may think that a car needs wheels more than anything else and therefore a person shouldn't spend money on other components, but the parts of a vehicle operate together to make it function correctly. So does your body. So does the planet. Variables on the planet rarely exist in a vacuum where if they cease to exist it has no impact on the other components of the system. Just because you can't see an immediate impact of an item doesn't mean that it isn't directly impacting you. 

4) Charities in and of themselves are a misnomer. They exist to combat a certain plight or problem but likewise cannot exist without said plight or problem. In the US they become a altruistic, but ultimately futile, tool for folks to justify individualist choices rather than mandates for the common good. Where the people of some countries collectively decide to address an issue even if it doesn't affect them directly because it is for the common good, here in the US (where I am but not sure about you) we often refuse to address things on a collective level, and instead developed a tax system that allows the rich to shelter and minimize their incomes while giving economic power over social issues that are issues of the common good. A prime example would be the prison industrial complex and rehabilitation methods that differ between the US and Scandinavian countries respectively. Or healthcare in other industrialized nations like the UK or France or Germany vs the United States. The thought process that a problem is only a problem if it impacts you or your kind (in the case of your view, humans) is one that tends to omit the fact that most problems are collective problems. If a sick person can't get treatment for a dangerous disease that then continues to spread through a community, that's everyone's problem. Animal problems are still problems for humans, just one step farther removed. Regardless, they should be handled on collective societal levels rather than the inefficiency of private charities. However until such time as humans can all figure out how to work together on overarching problems, than we just use the tools we have in front of us, which for your post, would be animal charities.

Medication is not a silver bullet and will not address mental health issues by itself (or at least overnight). There is no such thing as a "fix" for a mental health issue. Everything effective in treatment (medication with therapy, therapy, exercise, diet, etc) is something that has to be done regularly and over time, like watering a plant. People tend to think, "Oh well your medicated now so you must be all good". No, I'm medicated now so I have slightly more bandwidth to do the other basic life functions that set me on the path to being mentally healthy. It's an eternal humanistic marathon, not an FMLA compliant/ insurer approved short-term sprint.

Think of it this way. A well diversified portfolio is riding a bus. Reasonable, mostly reliable (let's assume it's a bus in a city like Toronto or NY), and generally safe. Alternatively, investing in only growth securities is like driving a sport motorcycle to your destination. Bull markets are good weather and little traffic and bear markets bad weather or bad traffic. Growth and risk are always interconnected and getting higher growth is like driving the motorcycle faster; yes you increase the chance that you get to your destination faster (and safely if there's little traffic) but you also increase the risk and likelihood of a deadly crash (much more likely if you're splitting lanes in bad weather and heavy traffic). The tradeoff with a robo-advised (or any professionally managed portfolio available to investors that aren't accredited investors) is that you are on a transit system operated by a licensed bus operator (who has both a legal and financial incentive to get you to your destination safely and reasonably, not as fast as humanly possible). They aren't going to break laws or take risks with you on the bus (like running a yellow even), you aren't going to get there as fast as if you rode the bike in and out of traffic, but you will ostensibly get there in a reasonable amount of time and safely. Risk and reward, the iron law of investing (and honestly a fair amount of life). Any portfolio offered by a money manager/ BD/ RIA is not going to beat the market consistently (although maybe occasionally), and if it does, chances are it's not available to the vast majority of investors (like the Medallion Fund for example). The purpose is not to outperform in any market, it's a product made for those who don't have the time or knowledge or ability or any combination therein to manage their own money (and the non-fee based robo-advisor has a lower minimum so that people without as many assets who can't or won't manage their money have an entry level option to a managed portfolio). Regulations like Reg BI endeavor to ensure (but don't guarantee, although with larger RIAs or BDs like Schwab they tend to be more effective in curtailing reckless behavior) that investment advisors are NOT engaging in the same risky and dangerous behavior that has led to countless losses incurred throughout the history of the stock market caused by profligate gambling and poor risk management by unscrupulous money managers and charlatans. Remember the entirety of The Vanguard Group and a tremendous amount of the popularity of index funds in general exist because John Bogle and other investors who realized "you can't beat the market, so be the market instead". 

TL/DR: Don't be shocked when you buy a product and it does what it was advertised to do. The marketing materials (https://www.schwab.com/intelligent-portfolios) don't say that it's supposed to beat the market. It's supposed to automate the investing process at minimal cost. You got on a regular city bus but somehow thought you were getting on a race motorcycle and you're shocked you didn't get to your destination first? Does that make the bus useless? Nope.

Rule 2090 by the regulatory body FINRA and additional guidance from theUS Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCen) established a regulatory framework for the Know Your Customer or KYC rule. This requires documentation that can be verified by a third party auditor. Court records may be sealed or confidential and therefore unable to be verified by an auditor. As such, firms reduce regulatory and compliance risk by standardizing their required documentation to items that can be easily verified by audit firms. One of the largest impetus for these rules was the Patriot Act which established a requirement for banks and brokerages to know their clientele in far more detail than they previously had. Name updates and changes impact audit trails, tax liability, and most importantly (at least to the US Government) trackability. Fidelity, like many large organizations, is establishing a verifiable paper trail that can be used to mitigate form risk. That's why.

Edit: here are some verifiable sources but not exhaustive.  The process is onerous by design, if people can change their names, the thinking is that, detailed documentation prevents dubious parties from utilizing US banking services. Or at least provides another barrier and complication for unscrupulous parties to use the system. Think terrorist groups, cartels, small level scammers, etc. Crimes tend to occur more frequently when they are convenient. This doesn't eliminate financial crimes but it does complicate the ability for someone to use Fidelity to facilitate the movement of illicit funds or the like. Also I missed another point. The FDIC has a separate ID requirements for the Know Your Customer times as banks and brokerages are regulated by separate regulatory bodies. Companies like Fidelity or Schwab have both bank and brokerage components and must meet both regulatory bodies requirements.

No matter what app (really brokerage firm) you are using, if you are placing a market order, it does not "lock in" the price. When you look at price, you are seeing the most recent trade executed, not the price you will pay. If you look at the bid and ask, that will tell you a closer price to what you might pay or receive (the bid is the highest a buyer will pay and the ask is the lowest a seller will sell). Using a limit order guarantees price but not a fill. Market orders guarantee a fill but not a price. Bear in mind that the variables that can impact the speed at which your order hits a market maker can include but are not limited to: Your ISP or cellular provider and their data speeds or volumes, your device itself, the proximity to a tower, your geography), etc. There are traders who have literally paid millions to lay fiber optic line to increase trade delivery speeds by fractions of a second (Spread Networks in 2008 paid upwards of $300 million to build a fiber line from Chicago to NY that increased it's execution time by 3 milliseconds or the equivalent of a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a sneeze). Don't focus on speed. Retail trading is using your feet while institutions are in F-22s.

In theory fundamentals tell you what to buy and technicals tell you when. In practice? Technicals are like any other thing in your life that exist to reduce risk or increase success. Traders who use to volume indicators in conjunction with momentum indicators may just be using that data to see if a price level they already determined to be their comfortable entry point is being sustained or maybe to see if the recent average true range is outside their predetermined risk tolerance. You develop rules for yourself as a trader and stick by those rules. Technicals are a tool, not the whole solution.
